title: Data Thinking, Lesson 1: Choosing a metric - and why the pretty ones are usually useless
subtitle: Telling a vanity metric from one that drives action, and the trap of turning a metric into a target
whyItMatters: Choosing the wrong metric is the most expensive mistake in analysis, because it happens before any calculation and no calculation can undo it. An organisation measuring the wrong thing will optimise in the wrong direction very efficiently, and usually only notices several quarters later.
openingQuestion: What separates a vanity metric from one that is genuinely useful?
openingOptions: A useful metric is always an absolute number, while a vanity metric is a percentage
A useful metric is one where, when it moves, somebody knows to do something differently
A useful metric is built from internal data, a vanity metric from external data
A useful metric is always harder to calculate than a vanity one
explanation: Cumulative sign-ups since launch is the classic vanity metric: it can only go up, so it always looks good, but nobody does anything differently when they look at it. Sign-ups that became active again this week is a different animal - it can fall as well as rise, and when it falls somebody has to find out why. The only test worth remembering: if this number gets worse, who does what?

realWorldExample.company: A bank measuring new accounts opened
realWorldExample.description: A common branch-network target is the number of accounts opened in the period. It is easy to measure, it rises steadily, and it looks excellent on a report. The problem is how easily it is gamed: staff open accounts for relatives and for customers with no real need, the target is hit, and the number of accounts with actual transactions does not move at all. Switch to measuring accounts still active after 90 days and the target becomes far harder to hit - but it starts reflecting what the bank actually needs.

quiz.question: Why is cumulative total users considered a vanity metric?
options: Because companies tend to report this number without much precision
Because it can only rise, so it signals nothing that would change anyone's action
Because collecting it demands a tracking system more complex and costly than others
Because professional investors these days have all stopped caring about this metric
quiz.explanation: A metric that moves in only one direction carries no information. Precision is not the issue - the number is usually accurate, and it is one of the cheapest things a company can count, so cost is not the issue either. What is worth measuring is the part that can move both ways: how many people came back, how many left during the period.

quiz.question: What does Goodhart's law say about metrics?
options: Every business metric tends to converge on the average value for its own industry
The more frequently a metric is measured, the more its accuracy gradually improves
Once a metric becomes a target, it stops being a good measure of what you want
The number of metrics tracked should be proportional to the headcount measuring them
quiz.explanation: This is why you have to ask how a metric can be gamed before attaching rewards or penalties to it. Measuring something more often does not make it a better measure, and nothing about the law concerns industry averages or how many metrics an organisation should keep. People always optimise exactly what is measured, even when doing so damages the real objective.

quiz.question: Why should a counter-metric accompany the main metric?
options: Because tracking two metrics at the same time raises the accuracy of both measurements
Because a counter-metric is usually easier to collect data for than the main one
Because current reporting standards require at least two measures per objective
Because it blocks optimising the main metric by sacrificing something else important
quiz.explanation: Measure how fast applications are processed without measuring the rework rate and processing really will get faster - by getting sloppier. Adding a second metric changes nothing about measurement accuracy, ease of collection is beside the point, and no reporting standard mandates the practice. A pair that has to improve together is far harder to game.

quiz.question: How does a leading metric differ from a lagging one?
options: A leading metric moves first and leaves time to act; a lagging one confirms the past
A leading metric is computed from forecast data, a lagging one from actual data
A leading metric is for the board, a lagging one is for the operating teams
A leading metric is measured daily, while a lagging one is always measured each quarter
quiz.explanation: Quarterly revenue is a lagging metric: by the time you know it, the quarter is over. Both kinds are computed from actual data, both are read at every level of an organisation, and the measurement frequency is a matter of practicality rather than definition. Customer meetings booked this week is a leading metric for that same revenue, and there is still time to adjust.

quiz.question: What does Goodhart's law warn about using a metric as a target?
options: The more precisely a metric measures, the harder its data is to collect
Once a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure
Every metric loses its meaning over time and has to be swapped out
A composite metric always hides the movement of its own components
quiz.explanation: When a bonus is tied to a number, people optimise that number rather than the thing it stands for. The other statements are either false or describe unrelated problems: precision and collection cost are not linked in that way, and aggregation hiding component movement is a separate issue entirely. This is why each headline metric should carry a counter-metric: push call volume and you have to watch the repeat-customer rate too.

keyTakeaways: The test: if this metric gets worse, who does what differently? If you cannot answer, do not measure it
A metric that only moves one way is a vanity metric - what is worth measuring is the part that can fall
Goodhart's law: once a metric becomes a target, it stops being a good measure
Always pair a metric with a counter-metric to block optimising by sacrificing something else
A leading metric still leaves time to act; a lagging one only confirms what already happened

practicePrompt.question: The customer service team is given a target of reducing the average handling time per call. What is the biggest risk?
options: Staff will end up overworked and the attrition rate will rise
Staff end calls before the issue is solved, so customers call back
The cost of running the call centre system will go up
Call-duration data is hard to measure with real accuracy
practicePrompt.explanation: This is Goodhart in practice: the target is hit, average handling time really does fall, but total call volume rises because the same issue gets called in repeatedly. The counter-metric needed here is first-call resolution - only when both improve together is the gain real.

summary.keyIdea: A good metric is one where, when it gets worse, somebody knows what to do
summary.commonMistake: Choosing a metric because it is easy to measure and looks good, rather than because it leads to action
summary.action: For each metric you track, write one sentence: if it fell 20%, who would do what next week?

application.title: What to do
application.message: Take your department's set of metrics and sort each one on two axes: can it move both ways or only one, and does it lead or merely confirm the result. The ones sitting in the one-way, confirm-only corner are candidates for dropping.
application.secondary: Then, for each metric that survives, ask one more question: if I wanted to cheat this number, how would I do it?

sections.text: Every technique in the previous stage assumed you already knew what you needed to measure. But choosing what to measure is the most important decision of all, and it is made before a single line of code is written.
Four questions for screening a metric

sections.title: The questions to ask before accepting a metric
sections.subtitle: Failing any one of them is reason enough to think again

concepts.def: The metric has to move up and down in response to someone's actions. A running cumulative total only goes one way, so it carries no signal.
A metric that belongs to nobody gets watched by nobody. Without an owner, however pretty it looks, it just sits on a report.
A leading metric moves first and leaves time to intervene. A lagging metric only confirms what has already happened. You need both, but do not confuse their roles.
Ask this before attaching rewards or penalties. People always optimise exactly what is measured, even when doing so wrecks the real objective.

left.label: Vanity metrics
left.text: Cumulative users, total views, total applications received. Always rising, always flattering on a slide, and nobody changes their behaviour on seeing them.

right.label: Metrics that drive action
right.text: 30-day repeat customer rate, average days to collect, share of applications requiring rework. They can fall, they have an owner, and when they worsen there is something to do.

sections.label: Pairing with a counter-metric
sections.text: Almost any metric taken alone can be gamed. The simplest defence is to pair it: speed with quality, growth with churn, sales with returns. Once two metrics have to improve at the same time, most of the shortcuts are closed off.

lines: No calculation rescues you from measuring the wrong thing. That decision comes before any tool.
The next lesson covers how a single average can conceal the entire truth.

sections.title: Putting numbers in to separate real metrics from vanity ones
sections.equation: A real metric ties to money: Revenue per active user = Revenue ÷ users who actually use it

example.title: An app advertising 'one million users'
example.calculation: Cumulative signups 1,000,000 · monthly active users 40,000 · paying 3,000 · monthly revenue VND 300m
example.result: Revenue per signup = VND 300 · per active user = VND 7,500 · per paying user = VND 100,000
example.explanation: One business, three figures more than 300 times apart, and only the first goes on the homepage. Cumulative signups is a vanity metric because it only ever rises - it cannot respond to anything that happens afterwards. The metric worth tracking is the one that can GO DOWN when the business does badly.
